Now on to what causes the "current ice age": Whenever a continent approaches one of the poles (Antarctica in this instance), it creates a polar ocean current that surrounds the continent and acts as a heat exchanger. Since the current circles the continent and never travels out of the polar regions, it stays cold. Other currents make "skin to skin contact" and the polar current heats up a little, while the other currents cool down. Where the polar current isn't making contact with other currents (say off the coast of South Africa, or Tierra del Fuego) they cool again due to the fact that the arctic and antarctic are cold. This band of water cools the Atlantic, the Pacific, and the Indian Oceans. It also helps drive the convection of the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans (cold water sinks, while warm water rises) that provides nutrients for the organisms close to the surface of the oceans.

If you go back in the geologic record, you'll see that the thermal maximums all occurred when there were no large land masses near the poles (or the land masses that were near the poles were part of super-continents where circumpolar currents cannot form) and thermal minimums occur when circumpolar currents form around large land masses on the polar regions.

The EC (as it came to be called) was a compromise because originally Congress was going to vote for the president, but there is a clear conflict of interest in having the legislative branch elect the president who is supposed to keep check over them. They were afraid of 'factions' in which a majority of the people would vote in self interest, against the rights of the minority (not used in a racial sense here) or the nation as a whole. (See federalist paper 10). It was Hamilton's Federalist Paper 68 that outlined what the EC was supposed to be. Afraid of the people directly electing a president, but wanting to maintain a "sense of the people" that the people would elect electors, who would be 1) elected by citizens on a district-by-district basis. 2) free to would exercise independent judgment when voting 3) candidates wouldn't pair together for Pres and V-P positions. Madison even drafted an amendment that electors would be done on a district-by-distrct basis.

But this isn't what happened. This isn't how we implement the EC today. The real problem is the winner-take-all system. All but two states award electorate votes on a winner take all basis. In addition, electors do not analyze or deliberate, they are puppets who pull a lever (for the most part).

Less populous states (smaller isn't quite accurate to say, as AK only has 3 votes) have a minimum of three votes. This is an artifact of each state having two senators and the number of electorates being based off the number of senators and representatives in congress. As the original plan was to have Congress elect the president, the count included a count equal to the number of senators.

However I challenge you to find anything that the intent of the framers of the constitution to include the number of senators in the count of electorate votes was based specifically on wanting to give the less populace states a slightly greater advantage on a voter-by-voter basis in electing the president. As i contend, it is an artifact of the compromise of having a senate, and not a specific motivation in how they decided on the number of members in the EC.

But the real problem isn't with the "all states get represented", the real failure is coming from the winner-take-all system. And this isn't what the founding fathers wanted. Electors were supposed to be elected on a district by district basis.
